pharm: Aminosteroid nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor end-plate to produce skeletal muscle paralysis; reversible by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors
tags: WARNING: administer only by clinicians skilled in intubation/ventilation
quick: Intubating dose 0.08-0.1 mg/kg IV bolus (intubation conditions in 2.5-3 min)
Use only if clearly needed; no human/animal reproduction data
Unknown if excreted in human milk; use caution
Well tolerated if dialyzed before surgery; consider lower initial dose in anephric emergencies
Prolonged recovery in cirrhosis/cholestasis; no specific dose recommendation
Peripheral nerve stimulator (twitch response); ensure ventilation and reversal agents available
summary: Vecuronium is an intermediate-duration aminosteroid nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent used intravenously as an adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation and provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation. It produces complete skeletal muscle paralysis, including the muscles of respiration, so mechanical ventilation and airway management are mandatory and it must be used only by clinicians experienced in intubation and ventilation. Vecuronium has NO analgesic, sedative, or anxiolytic effect and no effect on consciousness or the pain threshold, so it must always be accompanied by adequate anesthesia or sedation. Accidental administration of neuromuscular blockers can be fatal.
indications: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation
Skeletal muscle relaxation during mechanical ventilation

dosage.t: Intubation conditions in 2.5-3 min; block lasts ~25-30 min
dosage.n: 1.4-1.75 x ED90; pediatric 10-16 yr same mg/kg as adults

dosage.r: Maintenance of relaxation during prolonged surgery
dosage.t: First dose ~25-40 min after initial dose; then every ~12-15 min
dosage.n: No clinically important cumulative effect; use clinical criteria and twitch monitoring

dosage.r: After inhalation agent at steady state (>5 min)

dosage.n: Succinylcholine enhances effect/duration; delay vecuronium until succinylcholine wearing off

dosage.t: Start ~20-40 min after bolus, only after early spontaneous recovery
dosage.n: Titrate to ~90% twitch suppression; reduce rate 25-60% with enflurane/isoflurane

dosage.d: Slightly higher initial dose may be required
dosage.t: Supplementation slightly more often than adults

dosage.d: Moderately more sensitive on mg/kg basis than adults
dosage.t: Take ~1.5 times as long to recover
dosage.n: Not established <7 weeks of age; no continuous-infusion dosing in pediatrics

admin: Administer only by or under supervision of clinicians experienced with neuromuscular blocking agents and skilled in intubation/ventilation
Do not give unless facilities for intubation, artificial respiration, oxygen, and reversal agents are immediately available; be prepared to assist or control respiration
Always accompany with adequate anesthesia or sedation - vecuronium has no analgesic or sedative effect
Monitor muscle twitch response with a peripheral nerve stimulator to guide dosing
Reconstitute and dilute with compatible solutions (NS, D5W, D5/NS, Lactated Ringer's, sterile water); do NOT mix with alkaline solutions such as thiopental
Single-dose (preservative-free) reconstitution: refrigerate and use within 24 hours; discard unused portion
Inspect for particulate matter and discoloration before administration
Store with cap and ferrule intact to minimize wrong-product errors
moa: Vecuronium is a nondepolarizing (curariform) neuromuscular blocking agent that competes with acetylcholine for cholinergic (nicotinic) receptors at the motor end-plate, blocking neuromuscular transmission and producing skeletal muscle paralysis. The block is reversed by acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (neostigmine, edrophonium, pyridostigmine), usually with an anticholinergic such as atropine or glycopyrrolate. Vecuronium is about one-third more potent than pancuronium with shorter duration, has no clinically significant hemodynamic effects, and has no effect on consciousness, cerebration, or the pain threshold.

relative: Myasthenia gravis or myasthenic (Eaton-Lambert) syndrome - small doses may have profound effects
Prior anaphylactic reaction to any neuromuscular blocker (cross-reactivity reported)
Severe obesity or neuromuscular disease (airway/ventilatory problems)
Anephric emergency surgery (consider lower initial dose)
monitor: Degree of neuromuscular blockade by peripheral nerve stimulator
Adequacy of ventilation and oxygenation throughout

preg: Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted with vecuronium, and it is not known whether it can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. Vecuronium should be given to a pregnant woman only if clearly needed. In cesarean section reports following succinylcholine intubation, umbilical venous plasma concentrations were about 11% of maternal levels and mean 5-minute neonatal Apgar scores were >9. The action of neuromuscular blockers may be enhanced by magnesium salts given for toxemia of pregnancy.
lact: It is not known whether vecuronium is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk, caution should be exercised when vecuronium is administered to a nursing woman. Given single intraoperative use and rapid clearance, clinically significant infant exposure is unlikely.
renal: Vecuronium is well tolerated without clinically significant prolongation of neuromuscular block in patients with renal failure who have been optimally prepared for surgery by dialysis; recovery measurements do not differ significantly from healthy patients. Under emergency conditions in anephric patients some prolongation of blockade may occur, so a lower initial dose should be considered if the patient cannot be dialyzed before non-elective surgery.
hepatic: The liver plays a role in vecuronium metabolism and excretion, and experience in patients with cirrhosis or cholestasis shows prolonged recovery time (some recovery measurements may be doubled). Available data do not permit specific dosage recommendations in hepatic impairment; titrate carefully with neuromuscular monitoring.

major: Volatile inhalation anesthetics (enflurane, isoflurane, halothane) - enhance/prolong blockade; reduce dose (most prominent with enflurane and isoflurane)
Aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, bacitracin, polymyxin B, colistin, sodium colistimethate - may intensify or produce neuromuscular block
Succinylcholine (prior use) - enhances effect and duration; reduce vecuronium dose
moderate: Other nondepolarizing blockers (pancuronium, d-tubocurarine, metocurine, gallamine) - additive effect
Quinidine - may cause recurrent paralysis during recovery
minor: Thiobarbiturates, narcotic analgesics, nitrous oxide, droperidol - little or no increase in block intensity/duration
interactions.diagnostics: Acidosis enhances and alkalosis counteracts blockade; electrolyte imbalance (e.g. adrenal cortical insufficiency) may enhance or inhibit block. Do not mix with alkaline solutions (e.g. thiopental) - acid pH causes incompatibility

common: Extension of pharmacologic action beyond the needed period (skeletal muscle weakness)
Prolonged or profound skeletal muscle paralysis leading to respiratory insufficiency or apnea
serious: Prolonged paralysis, skeletal muscle weakness, and muscle atrophy after long-term ICU use to support mechanical ventilation
Hypersensitivity reactions: bronchospasm, hypotension and/or tachycardia, sometimes with urticaria or erythema
rare: Severe allergic reactions (anaphylactic/anaphylactoid), occasionally life-threatening or fatal
emergency: Respiratory arrest/apnea from paralysis (especially in an unintended patient) - manual or mechanical ventilation required

monitoring: Peripheral nerve stimulator to assess twitch response and degree of blockade (continuously in the ICU)
Continuous ventilation, oxygenation, and airway status
Adequacy of reversal - skeletal muscle tone and respiration before extubation
In the ICU: monitor neuromuscular transmission; do not give additional doses before a definite T1/first-twitch response
counsel: This medicine is given by an anesthesia/critical care team in the operating room or ICU; you will not self-administer it
It temporarily paralyzes muscles, including those for breathing, so a breathing machine will support you while it works
It does not relieve pain or cause sleep - separate anesthesia or sedation will keep you unconscious and comfortable
Tell your anesthesia team about any previous reaction to muscle relaxants or anesthetics and about myasthenia gravis or neuromuscular disease
Muscle weakness can occasionally last longer than expected, especially after prolonged ICU use
pk: First twitch depression ~1 min; good/excellent intubation conditions in 2.5-3 min (onset is dose-dependent)
Maximum neuromuscular blockade within 3-5 min of injection
Distribution ~4 min; elimination ~65-75 min (~35-40 min in late pregnancy)
Clinical block ~25-30 min; 25% recovery at ~25-40 min, 95% recovery at ~45-65 min after intubating dose
Store dry powder at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light; retain in carton until use
pearls: VENTILATION REQUIRED - vecuronium paralyzes all skeletal muscle including the diaphragm; mechanical/manual ventilation and airway control are mandatory
No analgesic/sedative effect - has no effect on consciousness or pain; ALWAYS combine with adequate anesthesia or sedation to avoid awareness during paralysis
Use only by clinicians skilled in intubation/ventilation with reversal agents (neostigmine/edrophonium/pyridostigmine + atropine/glycopyrrolate) immediately available
Accidental administration of neuromuscular blockers can be fatal - confirm the correct product and clearly label/communicate the dose
Monitor depth of block with a peripheral nerve stimulator; do not increase dose to speed onset (higher doses prolong duration)
Long-term ICU use can cause prolonged paralysis and disuse muscle weakness/atrophy, often first noticed at ventilator weaning
No clinically significant hemodynamic effects, unlike some other nondepolarizing relaxants
missed: Not applicable - vecuronium is administered by anesthesia/critical care clinicians as titrated intraoperative or ICU doses, not on a patient-managed schedule. Maintenance doses are given based on twitch monitoring and clinical need.
overdose: Overdose produces enhanced and prolonged neuromuscular block manifested as skeletal muscle weakness, decreased respiratory reserve, low tidal volume, or apnea. Primary treatment is maintaining a patent airway with manual or mechanical ventilation until full spontaneous respiration returns. Pyridostigmine, neostigmine, or edrophonium with atropine or glycopyrrolate usually antagonize the block once spontaneous recovery has begun; assess adequacy by muscle tone, respiration, and twitch response. Prompt reversal may fail in extreme debilitation, carcinomatosis, or with potentiating antibiotics/anesthetics. Effects of hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis on vecuronium levels are unknown.
